paragraphs: [Saadia] claimed that the written laws (al-sharāʾiʿ al-maktūba) are of two kinds: rational (ʿaqliyya) and report-based (samʿiyya).[{2}] The rational ones — even if they had not been mentioned in Scripture — God's servants could have arrived at by reason; hence even if there are similar-sounding expressions in the verbiage of their statement, this would not confound their reality, since reason returns to them, sifts and refines them, and ascertains them. The report-based ones, by contrast, owe their being-known to their being-set-down in a book; if their textual statement contains ambiguous wording, we are at a loss when multiple meanings press upon us, and we are forced to recur to the statement of one who witnessed the Messenger — so that those ambiguous wordings in the report-based commandments may be returned to the secure (the muḥkam). And reason itself rules that the Wise One does not leave His command and prohibition ambiguous: He Himself has said (Deut 30:11), "it is not hidden from thee," and the Wise One has testified to Himself that His [law] is clear and plain, as it says (Prov 8:9), "they are all right to him who understands."

He said: when one investigates, one finds seven foundational reasons (sabʿat uṣūl) in the report-based law that compel recurrence to naql. Each of them, considered in itself, is binding. The first: there are in Scripture commandments whose manner of being (kayfiyyāt) is not explained — for example, the fringes of garments, the sukkah, and the like. We do not know how, in detail, these are to be done. The second: there are commandments whose quantities (kammiyyāt) are not explained — for example, the terumah (priestly portion): "part of the herd" is mentioned, but no numerical quantity. Likewise the limits on the king's accumulation of wives, money, and horses (Deut 17:16–17): Scripture says "let him not multiply" each, but does not specify the upper bound. Quantity must be settled before quality, and is more urgent. The third: there are commandments whose time of incidence is not explained. Scripture has not given a sensible indicator of which day is the Sabbath, nor which day is Rosh Ḥodesh; we are referred to the transmission of the Messenger for these. The fourth: there are commandments whose substantive essence is not explained. Thus the nature of the works prohibited on the Sabbath is not articulated: Exod 20:10 says only "do no manner of work," without specifying what counts as work. Likewise the vessel that admits impurity (Lev 11:32): "every vessel" without specifying which sort.

The fifth: the people are in consensus that God (mighty and exalted) has appointed commandments not named in the Torah at all, let alone their quantity and quality. Examples: the obligatory three daily prayers, on whose obligation all are agreed but which are not in the text; the marriage-contract (ketuba), on whose necessity for marriage all are agreed but which is not in the text. There are many such — aḥkām that Scripture does not mention even minimally, but which necessity drives us to come to know. The sixth: historical chronology — the tārīkh of years and events from the cessation of prophecy down to our own day. This cannot be gained except through naql. By it we know how long the Second Temple stood and what happened during its existence, how its destruction took place, and so on from then to now. The seventh: our hope for the coming of the eschaton and what God will renew at the end of days. This is not securable for the community unless the community relies on the interpretation of the nāqilūn (the transmitters). For if the matter were entrusted to raʾy alone, anyone could claim that all the prophetic eschatological promises had already been fulfilled in the days of some earlier king (Zedekiah, etc.) — including the resurrection of the dead and the general bishārāt — and so all our hope would be nullified.

He said: it now falls to me to explain how these matters were transmitted from the prophets' reports. These māhiyyāt (essences), kammiyyāt (quantities), and kayfiyyāt (modalities) were observed by the community in the practice of the Messenger himself, forty years before the Torah was written. For the text shows that the Torah was written in the fortieth year of the wilderness: God commanded Moses, "write," and dictated to him word by word — from "In the beginning God created" (Gen 1:1) to "but thither thou shalt not pass" (Deut 34:4). He thus condensed for him the news of 2,488 years into that span. Such is the truth concerning the writing of the Torah: anyone who reads it has access to the historical and legal substance and to the first generation. The Messenger himself transmitted to the community all the laws and rulings that he was commanded with, since "he appointed for them captains of thousands and captains of hundreds" (Deut 1:15) to judge what came before them. It is inadmissible that he should command them to eat unleavened bread without specifying which grain it must be from; or to separate from impurities without explaining the limit of the man with the issue and the woman with the issue; and so on. By this necessity, the oral transmitted report must be forty years prior to the writing of the written.[{3}]

When the sons of Jacob were gathered together in the Holy Land, the king and the priest were preserving these oral reports and guarding them, especially in the presence of the prophets. When they were afflicted with the first calamity (the destruction of the First Temple) and the prophets had departed — the ancients (al-qudamāʾ) feared lest the hidden knowledge be forgotten; so they turned to its main heads (ʿuyūn) and recorded them, calling the result the Mishnah, and left out branches (furūʿ) in the hope that these would later be preserved by the inscribed main-heads. That state of affairs held until the second calamity (the Second Temple destruction) befell — a calamity fiercer than the first. At that point the disciples feared that what their predecessors had not inscribed might fall into desuetude, so they turned to it as well and inscribed it, calling the result the Talmud.

He said: a questioner might ask, How is it that the statements in the Mishnah and Talmud are ascribed to individuals — to so-and-so — rather than to the community as a whole? Answer: because those individuals are the ones who reported these things to the community. When they reported them, the community remembered them and bore witness to them. They are not the originators of the statements — only the transmitters. This is exactly like Scripture's ascription of the rule of Num 31:23 ("everything that may go through the fire") to Eleazar — who is named because he was the one who transmitted the rule, not because he originated it.

He said: a questioner might ask, How is it that there is disagreement among the transmitters in the Mishnah and Talmud? Answer: it is not real disagreement; it only seems so to the hearer at first. The disagreement reduces to three kinds: Kind 1: A sage appears to disagree with his colleague in order to draw out from him the depth of his knowledge — without genuine disagreement. So Moses appeared to be angry with Aaron and his sons regarding their burning of the goat of the sin-offering, in order to elicit what they knew, because he could not yet be sure they had not received the rule without true understanding.[{4}] Kind 2: A given matter was heard from the Messenger as having two licit modes — one being permitted, the other forbidden — and some sages took up the announcement of the permitted, others of the forbidden, and both are correct on their respective sides. So Scripture says (Deut 20:19), "thou shalt not destroy" the fruit-tree, and yet (v. 20), "but the tree which thou knowest to be no food-tree, thou mayest destroy and cut down." Likewise (Lev 22:12), "if the daughter of a priest be married to a stranger," she may not eat of the priestly portion; but (v. 13), "if the daughter of a priest be a widow …, of her father's bread she shall eat." There is no inconsistency: the two cases hold under different conditions. Kind 3: A sage heard a partial statement and took it for complete, while the others heard the full statement. When the first one reports his understanding, the others correct him: "we have heard the full statement, and it contains specifications of what you heard partially." Example: someone who reads Lev 19:19 ("and a garment of two kinds woven together") in isolation might suppose every mixture is forbidden; but when he reads the whole Torah, he finds at Deut 22:11 ("wool and linen together") the specification — only wool and linen are forbidden.

He said: when these transmitters of knowledge were compelled to admit that certain unwritten elements of the report-based laws are needed, they said: "Yes, the Wise One left these unwritten because He referred us to qiyās." (We have already mentioned what we said in critique of qiyās, and demonstrated its corruption.) He then said: and some of them make the non-acceptance of part of the community a critique of the naql-claim — meaning, those who refuse to acknowledge the oral tradition. We reply: if his reasoning were sound, the non-acceptance of the written by some would equally be a critique of the written Torah. And some make the failure of part of the community to memorize the transmitted oral tradition into a critique against the tradition; but the same reasoning would condemn the written Torah, since some have failed to memorize it. ---
